The frequency attenuation that makes π go down is uncontroversial and it is the same mechanism that makes S go down.

Take a truly segregating VCF site with k true derived copies in the 2N panel. After independent per-haplotype quality filtering with retention probability r<1 the derived copies are retained independently. The site is still seen as segregating in the imputed alignment iff at least one of those k copies survives in its sample, i.e.

Pr{site survives | k}=1-(1-r)^k =1-q^k

with q=1-r the per-haplotype loss probability. The loss probability is >0 for every finite k and is a constant in N. The expected number of segregating sites that survive is therefore

E[S_obs]=∑_{k≥1} E[N_k] [1-q^k]

where under the infinite sites model E[N_k]=θ/k. Hence

E[S_obs]=θ∑_{k≥1}1/k - θ∑_{k≥1}q^k/k = S_true - θ[-log(1-q)] < S_true

for any q>0. The second term is the expected number of sites that become monomorphic reference after reference imputation because every carrier in the panel happens to be one of the filtered minority in its sample. It is strictly positive as soon as a substantial minority of calls is removed per sample.

The B arguments that Pr{loss}=q^{k}→0 rely on k=2Np→∞ for a fixed p>0. That is true for common alleles, but the site-frequency spectrum is dominated by rare alleles. For each fixed k the loss probability q^k is constant in N and the class k=1,2,… is always present. The condition “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ is a statement about the raw VCF, not about the post-filter, post-imputation alignment. After imputation a true derived allele that is filtered in the only sample that carries it is written as reference everywhere, so the site disappears from S and contributes zero pairwise differences.

Hence on the ascertained VCF set

E[ p_obs ] = r p_true < p_true

so 2p_obs(1-p_obs) < 2p_true(1-p_true) site by site, and

E[π_obs] < π_true

with a systematic downward attenuation that persists as N grows. At the same time

E[S_obs] < S_true

so E[θ_W,obs]=E[S_obs]/a_n < θ_W,true for every finite, albeit arbitrarily large, sample. The bias in S vanishes only in the formal n→∞ limit relative to log n, but the absolute expected loss θ[-log(1-q)] remains >0 in any realisable data set, and the bias is downward in practice.

Reference imputation therefore systematically removes variation both from the count of segregating sites that underlies Watterson’s θ_W and from the frequency-weighted pairwise differences that define π. Both statistics are downward biased under the described per-sample random deletion + reference imputation scheme.

union $V$ of variant positions that are entered in the VCFs.  For a site

haplotypes and let $r=1-f<1$ be the per-haplotype retention probability
after the random low-quality filter.  A true derived copy is seen as
derived with probability $r$ and, if it is deleted, it is imputed to the
reference allele.  On a haplotype

$$
X_{i}=Y_{i}R_{i},\qquad E[X_{i}]=E[Y_{i}]E[R_{i}]=p_{i}r,
$$

so that the observed derived frequency is attenuated

$$
p_{i}^{obs}=p_{i}r<p_{i}\qquad 0<p_{i}<1,
$$

and for two independent haplotypes

$$
E\big[(X_{i}-X_{j})^{2}\big]=2p_{i}r\!\left[1-p_{i}r\right]
<2p_{i}\!\left[1-p_{i}\right] .
$$

Hence on every truly segregating ascertained site

$$
\pi_{i}^{obs}=2p_{i}^{obs}\!\left(1-p_{i}^{obs}\right)
<2p_{i}\!\left(1-p_{i}\right)=\pi_{i}^{true},
$$

and after averaging over $V$

$$
\hat\pi_{obs}=|V|^{-1}\sum_{i\in V}\pi_{i}^{obs}
<|V|^{-1}\sum_{i\in V}\pi_{i}^{true} .
$$

The reference imputation turns a true derived copy into a reference copy
with probability $f>0$; the pairwise difference is therefore
systematically deflated and the deflation survives as $n\to\infty$.

\pi_{true}$.

segregating site $p_{i}>0$ is observed as monomorphic only if every
derived copy in the $2n$ haplotypes is deleted in its respective
sample,

$$
{\rm Pr}\{S_{i}^{obs}=0\mid p_{i}>0\}
 =\bigl[1-p_{i}r\bigr]^{2n}\approx\exp\!\big[-2np_{i}r\big]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0  .
$$

For a fixed $p_{i}>0$, $2np_{i}\to\infty$ and $ \Pr\{{\rm loss}\}=f^{\,2np_{i}}
\to0$.  With an arbitrarily large panel every truly segregating site in
the ascertained union $V$ retains at least one observed derived copy with
probability one, and by hypothesis no site is completely missing across
the panel.  Hence

$$
S_{obs}=\sum_{i\in V}{\bf1}\{p_{i}^{obs}>0\}\xrightarrow{p}|V|
=S_{true},
$$

and

$$
\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}\xrightarrow{p}
S_{true}/a_{n}=\hat\theta_{W}^{true}
$$

on the set $V$ that is actually examined.  Up to the $o(1)$ loss of the
very rarest singletons the $S$-based statistic is asymptotically
insensitive to the random, genotype-independent deletion and reference
imputation, whereas the frequency-dependent statistic $\pi$ is
systematically down-weighted by the factor $r$ on the whole site-frequency
spectrum.

nucleotide diversity downwards while Watterson’s $S/a_{n}$ estimator is
asymptotically unbiased.  The usual genome-wide per-base ascertainment
to $V$ inflates both estimators with respect to a true whole-genome

The data that are actually analysed are the union

$V=\{s: s{\rm \;is\;present\;in\;at\;least\;one\;VCF}\}$

with reference imputation for every missing call.  Let $r\in(0,1]$ be the
per-haplotype retention probability for a true derived copy and let
$p_{i}>0$ be the true derived frequency at $i\in V$ in the $2N$
haplotypes.  On a haplotype

$X_{i}=Y_{i}R_{i},\qquad Y_{i}\sim {\rm Bern}(p_{i}),\;R_{i}\sim {\rm Bern}(r)$

independently, so that with the reference imputation

$E[p_{i}^{obs}]=E[X_{i}]=rp_{i}<p_{i}$ .

For two independent haplotypes

$E[{\rm diff}_{i}^{obs}]=2p_{i}^{obs}(1-p_{i}^{obs})
      =2rp_{i}\bigl[1-rp_{i}\bigr]
      <2p_{i}(1-p_{i})=E[{\rm diff}_{i}^{true}]$

for every $0<p_{i}<1$, with strict inequality.  Hence on $V$

$\hat\pi_{obs}=|V|^{-1}\sum_{i}2\hat p_{i}^{obs}(1-\hat p_{i}^{obs})
      <|V|^{-1}\sum_{i}2p_{i}(1-p_{i})=\pi_{true},$

and the attenuation $p_{i}\to rp_{i}$ persists as $N\to\infty$.  Pairwise
nucleotide diversity is a frequency weighted statistic and it is
systematically depressed by the reference imputation of the randomly
deleted derived copies.  In the rare-allele regime $p_{i}\ll1$,
$\pi_{obs}\approx r\,\pi_{true}$.

Watterson’s statistic depends only on presence/absence of a derived
allele,

$\hat\theta_{W}=S/a_{N},\qquad 
S=\sum_{i}{\bf1}\{p_{i}^{obs}>0\}.$

A truly segregating site $p_{i}>0$ is lost from $S$ only if all
$K_{i}\approx2Np_{i}$ derived copies are deleted in their respective
haplotypes.  With per-haplotype deletion probability $q=1-r$,

$\Pr\{p_{i}^{obs}=0\mid p_{i}>0\}=q^{K_{i}}\to0$ as $N\to\infty$

for any fixed $p_{i}>0$.  With the sample size taken arbitrarily large
and the stipulation that no SNV is completely missing across the panel,
$\Pr\{p_{i}^{obs}>0\mid p_{i}>0\}\to1$ and

$E[S_{obs}]=\sum_{i}\bigl[1-q^{K_{i}}\bigr]\to\sum_{i}1=S_{true}$

on the ascertained set $V$.  Hence $S_{obs}\to S_{true}$ in probability
and

$E[\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}]=S_{obs}/a_{N}\to S_{true}/a_{N}
      =\hat\theta_{W}^{true}$

on $V$.  The binary segregating/non-segregating information is
asymptotically preserved by random per-sample deletion followed by
reference imputation; only the frequency information on which $\pi$
depends is attenuated.  Up to the usual $o(1)$ loss of the very rarest
alleles $\hat\theta_{W}$ is asymptotically unbiased on the examined
variant set, whereas $\hat\pi$ remains permanently down-biased by the
reference imputation.

Finite $N$ the loss $1-(1-q)^{k}$ does make $E[S_{obs}]<S_{true}$ for the
rarest alleles, i.e. a practical downward finite-sample bias in
$\theta_{W}$, but in the $N\to\infty$ idealisation adopted here the
site-presence statistic is retained and the frequency statistic is the
one that is systematically deflated. This is the usual
reference-imputation bias: $\pi$ is biased low, Watterson’s $S/a_{n}$
is asymptotically robust.

Watterson’s estimator uses presence/absence only, θ̂_W=S/a_n. Disagreement in the thread concerns the infinite-sites site frequency spectrum. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The VCF union $U$ is the set of ascertained variant sites. Per haplotype retention $r<1$, deletion $q=1-r>0$, imputation to reference gives observed derived indicator $X_i=Y_iR_i$ with $E[X_i]=r p_i$ and $p_i^{obs}=r p_i<p_i$. Hence

$E[{\rm diff}_{i}^{obs}]=2rp_i(1-rp_i)<2p_i(1-p_i)$

site by site. Nucleotide diversity $\pi$ is a frequency-weighted sum, so $\hat\pi_{obs}<\hat\pi_{true}$ with a persistent $r$-shrinkage that survives $n\to\infty$. In the rare regime $p_i\ll1$, $\pi_{obs}\approx r\pi_{true}$. That downward bias of $\pi$ is undisputed.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence: $\hat\theta_W=S/a_n$. A truly segregating site with $k_i=2np_i$ true derived copies is lost only if all copies are filtered, $\Pr\{S_i^{obs}=0\}=q^{k_i}$. For any fixed $p_i>0$, $k_i\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and $q^{k_i}\to0$. With the “no completely missing SNV’’ condition the union $U$ is the set of $p_i>0$ sites, so $E[S_{obs}]=\sum_i[1-q^{k_i}]\to\sum_i1=S_{true}$ and $\hat\theta_W^{obs}\to\hat\theta_W^{true}$ on $U$. The binary segregating/non-segregating status is asymptotically preserved, whereas the frequency information used by $\pi$ is permanently thinned.

The split in the discussion is about the infinite-sites frequency spectrum. The B camp treats the $n\to\infty$ limit pointwise for fixed $p>0$. The C camp notes that under the neutral spectrum $E[N_k]=\theta/k$ the expected number of sites erased is $E[\Delta S]=\sum_{k\ge1}\theta/k\,q^{k}= \theta[-\log(1-q)]>0$, and the loss probability for singletons/doubletons $q^{k}$ is a non-zero constant. For $k=O(1)$ the loss $1-(1-q)^k>0$ does not vanish with $n$, so in absolute expectation $E[S_{obs}]<S_{true}$ and $E[\hat\theta_W]<\hat\theta_W$ in any finite, arbitrarily large sample. The relative loss $\Delta S/S_{true}\sim[-\log(1-q)]/\log n\to0$, i.e. the bias vanishes relatively in the strict $n\to\infty$ idealisation but remains positive in practice for the rare tail that dominates human $S$.

Ascertainment to the variant set $U$ inflates both statistics on a genome-wide per-base scale; the comparison above is per ascertained site. The textbook reference-imputation story is therefore $\pi$ downward biased by $p\to rp$, Watterson’s $S/a_n$ asymptotically robust on $U$. The finite-sample / infinite-sites nuance makes both estimators formally downward biased in expectation, with the $\theta_W$ bias vanishing relatively as $n\to\infty$ while the $\pi$ bias persists. This is the source of the B vs C disagreement in the round.

After quality filtering a true derived allele is retained per haplotype with probability r =1-q<1 independent across haplotypes, and every deleted call is imputed to reference. Hence for a true derived frequency p>0 E[p_obs|p]=p r , p_obs

0; in the rare-allele regime E[π_obs]≈r E[π_true]. Watterson’s estimator is θ_W=S/a_n, S=∑1{p_i^obs>0}. A truly segregating site p_i>0 with k_i≈2Np_i derived copies is lost from S only if every copy is filtered: Pr{S_i^obs=0|p_i>0}=q^{k_i}. For any fixed p_i>0, k_i→∞ as N→∞ so q^{k_i}→0. With the “no completely missing SNV’’ condition the set V is the set of sites with p_i>0. Then E[S_obs]=∑[1-q^{k_i}] →∑1=S_true in probability, so on the ascertained variant set S_obs→S_true and θ_W^obs→θ_W^true in the large-N limit. Presence/absence of a polymorphism is asymptotically preserved by random per-sample deletion + reference imputation; only the frequency information needed for π is thinned. The split in the deliberation is the finite-sample / infinite-sites caveat. reflection_text.6:
The shared mechanism is now unanimous. Per haplotype retention r<1, deletion independent of true genotype, missing set ref-imputed. Observed derived indicator X=Y R, so E[X]=p r < p. Hence for any site 0<p<1

E[diff_obs]=2pr(1-pr) < 2p(1-p)=E[diff_true]

and

π_obs =2p_obs(1-p_obs) < 2p(1-p)

with the attenuation persisting as n→∞. Reference imputation systematically turns true derived copies into reference matches, so nucleotide diversity is permanently downward biased by the constant r factor. In the rare-variant regime π_obs≈r π_true.

The disagreement is Watterson S/a_n.

Presence/absence argument: a truly segregating ascertained site with k=2Np derived copies is lost from S only if all k copies are filtered in their own haplotypes. Pr[loss|p>0]=q^{k} with q=1-r. For any fixed p>0, k→∞ as n→∞ and q^{k}→0. With the “no completely missing SNV’’ condition the union V of VCF sites is the set of sites with p>0. Hence

E[S_obs]= Σ_i[1-q^{k_i}] → Σ_i1 = S_true

in probability, and θ_W^{obs}=S_obs/a_n → θ_W^{true} on V. The S-based estimator depends only on presence/absence, so the binary segregating/non-segregating information is asymptotically preserved while the frequency information underlying π is not. This is the B camp, 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8.

Counter-argument for downward bias of S: even with n→∞ the infinite-sites frequency spectrum continually replenishes k=O(1) sites. E[N_k]=θ/k. Loss per k-copy site is q^{k}>0, so

E[ΔS]= Σ_{k≥1} θ/k q^{k}=θ[-log(1-q)]>0

and E[S_obs]= Σ θ/k[1-q^{k}]<S_true. The per-site loss probability q^{k}→0 only for fixed p>0, not for the k=O(1) tail that dominates S in humans. Per-sample random deletion + reference imputation therefore erases the last observed copy of rare sites in expectation, giving a downward bias in S and hence θ_W for any finite, arbitrarily large panel. This is the C camp, 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7.

Further nuance: fixed-derived sites p=1 relative to reference. On a strict set-theoretic definition reference imputation creates artefact polymorphism at f=1 sites: Pr[site appears segregating|p=1]=(1-(1-r)^{2n})→1 and E[π|p=1]=2r(1-r)>0. In that strict sense S_obs=S_true+S_{p=1} would be inflated and π also inflated on that component. The textbook idealisation used by the B camp is 0<p<1 for all sites in V.

Ascertainment per V also matters: on a per-base genome-wide scale conditioning on the pre-ascertained polymorphic set V inflates both estimators relative to a true per-base expectation; the imputation effect is separate from that ascertainment inflation.

Current synthesis: on the ascertained variant set V and in the n→∞ limit stated in the problem, the binary segregating information asymptotically survives random genotype-independent deletion + reference imputation, so θ_W is asymptotically unbiased on V while π is permanently down-biased by the factor r. Finite-sample/infinite-sites reasoning gives a persistent expected loss of rare segregating sites, i.e. a practical downward bias in both S and π, which explains the split. The intended textbook statement is B: only π is biased downward, Watterson is asymptotically robust on V, with the finite-n rare-allele caveat that makes a C answer defensible in practice.

reflection_text.10:
The VCF union $U$ is the set of ascertained variant sites. Per haplotype retention $r<1$, deletion $q=1-r>0$, imputation to reference gives observed derived indicator $X_i=Y_iR_i$ with $E[X_i]=r p_i$ and $p_i^{obs}=r p_i<p_i$. Hence

$E[{\rm diff}_{i}^{obs}]=2rp_i(1-rp_i)<2p_i(1-p_i)$

site by site. Nucleotide diversity $\pi$ is a frequency-weighted sum, so $\hat\pi_{obs}<\hat\pi_{true}$ with a persistent $r$-shrinkage that survives $n\to\infty$. In the rare regime $p_i\ll1$, $\pi_{obs}\approx r\pi_{true}$. That downward bias of $\pi$ is undisputed.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence: $\hat\theta_W=S/a_n$. A truly segregating site with $k_i=2np_i$ true derived copies is lost only if all copies are filtered, $\Pr\{S_i^{obs}=0\}=q^{k_i}$. For any fixed $p_i>0$, $k_i\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and $q^{k_i}\to0$. With the “no completely missing SNV’’ condition the union $U$ is the set of $p_i>0$ sites, so $E[S_{obs}]=\sum_i[1-q^{k_i}]\to\sum_i1=S_{true}$ and $\hat\theta_W^{obs}\to\hat\theta_W^{true}$ on $U$. The binary segregating/non-segregating status is asymptotically preserved, whereas the frequency information used by $\pi$ is permanently thinned.

The split in the discussion is about the infinite-sites frequency spectrum. The B camp treats the $n\to\infty$ limit pointwise for fixed $p>0$. The C camp notes that under the neutral spectrum $E[N_k]=\theta/k$ the expected number of sites erased is $E[\Delta S]=\sum_{k\ge1}\theta/k\,q^{k}= \theta[-\log(1-q)]>0$, and the loss probability for singletons/doubletons $q^{k}$ is a non-zero constant. For $k=O(1)$ the loss $1-(1-q)^k>0$ does not vanish with $n$, so in absolute expectation $E[S_{obs}]<S_{true}$ and $E[\hat\theta_W]<\hat\theta_W$ in any finite, arbitrarily large sample. The relative loss $\Delta S/S_{true}\sim[-\log(1-q)]/\log n\to0$, i.e. the bias vanishes relatively in the strict $n\to\infty$ idealisation but remains positive in practice for the rare tail that dominates human $S$.

Ascertainment to the variant set $U$ inflates both statistics on a genome-wide per-base scale; the comparison above is per ascertained site. The textbook reference-imputation story is therefore $\pi$ downward biased by $p\to rp$, Watterson’s $S/a_n$ asymptotically robust on $U$. The finite-sample / infinite-sites nuance makes both estimators formally downward biased in expectation, with the $\theta_W$ bias vanishing relatively as $n\to\infty$ while the $\pi$ bias persists. This is the source of the B vs C disagreement in the round.
reflection_text.1:
The discussion remains split on the large-n limit vs the infinite-sites frequency spectrum.

*Observed frequency attenuation.* On the VCF union $V$ a per-haplotype retention probability $r<1$ with reference imputation gives $E[X_i]=Y_i R_i$, $E[p^{obs}]=r p$, $E[p^{obs}]<p$. Hence for a pair
$E[{\rm diff}^{obs}]=2pr(1-pr)<2p(1-p)$ and
$\pi_i^{obs}=2p_i^{obs}(1-p_i^{obs})<2p_i(1-p_i)$ site by site. Averaging over $V$ $\hat\pi_{obs}$ is systematically down-weighted, $\approx r\hat\pi_{true}$ for rare alleles, and the deflation persists as $n\to\infty$. This is agreed.

*Presence/absence.* A site with $k_i=2np_i$ true derived copies is lost from $S$ only if all $k_i$ copies are filtered:
$\Pr\{S_i^{obs}=0\mid p_i>0\}=q^{k_i}$ with $q=1-r$. For a fixed $p_i>0$, $k_i\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and $q^{k_i}\to0$, so
$E[S_{obs}]=\sum_{i}[1-q^{k_i}]\to\sum_{i}1=S_{true}$ on the ascertained set $V$. Hence in the textbook $n\to\infty$ idealisation $\hat\theta_W^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_n\to S_{true}/a_n$, i.e. Watterson’s $S/a_n$ is asymptotically preserved while $\pi$ is permanently $r$-shrunk. This is the $B$ camp: only $\pi$ is biased, $\theta_W$ asymptotically unbiased on $V$.

*Finite-spectrum counter.* The loss probability is $>0$ for the rare tail where $k=O(1)$. Under infinite sites $E[N_k]=\theta/k$ and
$E[\Delta S]=\sum_k E[N_k]q^k =\theta\sum_k q^k/k =-\theta\log(1-q)>0$.
The expected number of segregating sites erased by reference imputation is therefore constant in $N$ and $E[S_{obs}]<S_{true}$ for any finite $n$, the bias being driven by singletons/doubletons that are replenished as $n$ grows. The same thinning gives $E[p^{obs}]=rp$ and downward bias of $\pi$. This is the $C$ camp: both $S$ and $\pi$ are downward biased in expectation, the $q^{k}\to0$ for fixed $p$ being a pointwise limit that does not remove the mass at $k=O(1)$.

Additional nuance noted: conditioning on the variant union $V$ gives the usual ascertainment upward bias per base pair for both statistics; strict set-theoretic treatment of fixed-derived sites $p=1$ would create artefactual polymorphism under reference imputation, inflating $S$ and $\pi$ on that component. The problem states “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ and “number of samples arbitrarily large’’, which is the wording that motivates the large-$n$ $B$ statement, with the finite-$n$ $C$ statement being the realistic rare-allele caveat. The persistent belief is the textbook large-$n$ frequency-vs-presence distinction: $\pi$ is permanently deflated by reference imputation, $\theta_W$ is asymptotically robust on the ascertained VCF set, with the acknowledged finite-sample downward loss of $S$ for the $k=O(1)$ tail.

reflection_text.19:
The data are the union V of SNV positions present in at least one VCF. After per-haplotype random deletion of a fraction 1−r of true derived calls, every missing call is imputed to the reference allele. On a true biallelic site with derived frequency p>0 in 2N haplotypes

E[p_obs]=p r , p_obs<p,

so for two independent haplotypes

E[diff_obs]=2pr[1−pr] < 2p(1−p)=E[diff_true].

Hence π_obs = L⁻¹ Σ 2p_obs(1−p_obs) < L⁻¹ Σ 2p(1−p)=π_true site-wise, and the downward attenuation persists as N→∞ because the per-haplotype retention r is constant. Reference imputation systematically turns filtered derived copies into reference-reference matches; π is frequency dependent and is permanently down-biased.

Watterson’s estimator uses only presence/absence: \hatθ_W = S/a_n, S = Σ 1{p_obs>0}. A site with k=2Np true derived copies is lost from S iff all k copies are filtered: Pr{loss|k}= q^{k}, q=1−r. For any fixed p>0, k→∞ as N→∞ and q^{k}→0. With the “no completely missing SNV’’ ascertainment, every site in V has p>0 in the panel, so

E[S_obs]= Σ [1−q^{k_i}] → Σ1 = S_true

in probability, and \hatθ_W^{obs}=S_obs/a_n → S_true/a_n on the ascertained set V in the N→∞ idealisation. The binary segregating/non-segregating information is asymptotically preserved while the allele-frequency information is thinned.

Disagreement in the current round: colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7 stress the infinite-sites spectrum. Expected number of sites lost = Σ θ/k q^{k}=θ[−log(1−q)]>0, so in expectation S_obs < S_true for the k=O(1) rare tail that dominates S in humans. They argue both θ_W and π are downward biased in practice. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,8 argue the N→∞ idealisation intended by “arbitrarily large samples’’ makes q^{k}→0 pointwise for fixed p>0, so θ_W is asymptotically unbiased on V while π remains permanently down-biased.

The problem explicitly states the number of samples is arbitrarily large, favouring the asymptotic large-N idealisation where site-presence is retained and only the frequency-dependent statistic is deflated. Finite-sample rare-allele loss remains a practical source of downward bias in S/θ_W, which is the source of the C-both-biased position. The textbook reference-imputation bias quoted is B. Only π is biased, Watterson’s S-based estimator is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained variant set; the remaining ascertainment to V inflates both estimators on a genome-wide per-base scale, and the f=1 fixed-derived edge case would artefactually inflate S under a strict set-theoretic definition.

On the VCF union $V$ let $r<1$ be the per-haplotype retention probability and
$q=1-r>0$ the per-haplotype deletion probability.  After deletion a deleted
derived copy is written as reference so for a true derived indicator $Y_i$
and a retention indicator $R_i$, $Y_i\perp R_i$,

$X_i=Y_iR_i$ ,   $E[X_i\mid Y_i]=rY_i$ ,

so that on a site with true derived frequency $p>0$

$E[p^{\rm obs}\mid p]=r p<p$

and for two independent haplotypes

$E[{\rm diff}^{\rm obs}\mid p]=2rp\!\left[1-rp\right]
<2p(1-p)=E[{\rm diff}^{\rm true}\mid p]$

for every $0<p<1$.  Hence site by site

$\pi_i^{\rm obs}=2p_i^{\rm obs}\!\left(1-p_i^{\rm obs}\right)
<2p_i\!\left(1-p_i\right)=\pi_i^{\rm true}$

and on $V$

reference-imputation effect being the down bias of $\pi$.

18.text:
The imputed indicator on a haplotype is $X_{i}=Y_{i}R_{i}$ with $Y_{i}\sim
{\rm Bern}(p)$ the true derived indicator and $R_{i}\sim{\rm Bern}(r)$,
$r=1-q<1$, the per-haplotype retention indicator, $Y_{i}\perp R_{i}$.
After reference imputation

${\rm E}[p^{obs}\mid p]=r p<p\,,\qquad 
{\rm E}[{\rm diff}^{obs}\mid p]=2rp\,[1-rp]<2p(1-p) $

for every $0<p<1$.  Hence on every truly segregating ascertained site

$\pi^{obs}_{i}=2p^{obs}_{i}(1-p^{obs}_{i})<2p_{i}(1-p_{i})=\pi^{true}_{i}$

and on the union $V$ of VCF sites

${\rm E}[\hat\pi_{obs}]
 =|V|^{-1}\sum_{i}2rp_{i}[1-rp_{i}]
 <|V|^{-1}\sum_{i}2p_{i}(1-p_{i})={\rm E}[\hat\pi_{true}]$.
The $p\mapsto rp$ thinning is frequency dependent and persists for all $n$,
in the rare regime $E[\pi^{obs}]\approx rE[\pi^{true}]$.  Reference
imputation turns every filtered derived copy into a reference match, so
pairwise nucleotide diversity is systematically down weighted.

Watterson’s statistic uses presence/absence only,
$\hat\theta_{W}=S/a_{n}$, $S=\sum_{s}{\bf1}\{p_{s}^{obs}>0\}$.
For a truly segregating site with $k_{s}=2np_{s}$ true derived copies

${\rm Pr}\{p_{s}^{obs}=0\mid p_{s}>0\}=q^{\,k_{s}}$.

For any fixed $p_{s}>0$, $k_{s}\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and
$q^{k_{s}}\to0$.  With the “no completely missing SNV’’ ascertainment the
site set $V$ is the set of sites with $p_{s}>0$ and

${\rm E}[S_{obs}]=\sum_{s\in V}\!\left[1-q^{k_{s}}\right]\to\sum_{s\in V}1
=S_{true},\qquad S_{obs}\xrightarrow{P}S_{true}$,

so that on the ascertained VCF set

$\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}\xrightarrow{P}S_{true}/a_{n}
=\hat\theta_{W}^{true}$.

The binary segregating/non-segregating information which defines $S$ is
asymptotically preserved by random genotype independent deletion followed
by reference imputation, whereas the frequency information which defines
$\pi$ is permanently attenuated by the $r$ factor.  In the $n\to\infty$
idealisation the classic reference-imputation bias is a downward bias of
nucleotide diversity with Watterson’s $S/a_{n}$ essentially unbiased on the
ascertained variant set.  Finite-$n$ the $k=O(1)$ tail gives a small
$O(1)$ downward $S$ loss, the relative loss vanishing as $n\to\infty$.
This is the usual presence versus frequency robustness.

In particular, per variable site, $\pi$ is permanently down biased by
reference imputation whereas $\hat\theta_{W}$ is asymptotically robust
on $V$. ∎

20.text:
On the union $V$ of sites that enter the VCF let $p_{i}>0$ be the true
derived frequency in the $2n$ phased haplotypes and let $r<1$ be the
per-haplotype retention probability after the random low-quality filter.
A deleted derived copy is written as reference, so on a haplotype

$$
X_{i}=Y_{i}R_{i},\qquad E[X_{i}\mid Y_{i}=1]=r,
$$

and with $Y_{i}\perp R_{i}$

$$
E[p_{i}^{obs}\mid p_{i}]=r p_{i}<p_{i},\qquad 0<p_{i}<1 .
$$

Hence for two independent haplotypes

$$
E\big[(X_{i}-X_{j})^{2}\mid p_{i}\big]=2pr\bigl[1-pr\bigr]
   <2p(1-p)=E\big[(Y_{i}-Y_{j})^{2}\mid p_{i}\big]
$$

site by site.  The observed heterozygosity is therefore

$$
\pi_{i}^{obs}=2p_{i}^{obs}\bigl(1-p_{i}^{obs}\bigr)
     <2p_{i}(1-p_{i})=\pi_{i}^{true},\qquad 0<p_{i}<1,
$$

and on the ascertained set

$$
\hat \pi_{obs}=|V|^{-1}\sum_{i\in V}2\hat p_{i}^{obs}
\bigl(1-\hat p_{i}^{obs}\bigr)
<|V|^{-1}\sum_{i\in V}2p_{i}(1-p_{i}) .
$$

The $p\to pr$ thinning is a constant frequency-dependent attenuation.
In the rare allele regime $p_{i}\ll1$, $E[\pi_{i}^{obs}]\simeq r\,
E[\pi_{i}^{true}]$, and the down shift persists for every $n$ and for
$n\to\infty$.  Reference imputation turns every filtered derived copy
into a reference match, so pairwise differences are systematically
under-counted.  $\pi$ is frequency weighted and is permanently deflated
by the reference imputation.

Presence/absence is different.  Let $K_{i}=2np_{i}$ be the true number of
derived copies at $i$.  The site is lost from the segregating-site count
iff all $K_{i}$ copies are filtered in their own samples,

$$
\Pr\{p_{i}^{obs}=0\mid p_{i}>0\}=q^{K_{i}},\qquad q=1-r .
$$

For any fixed $p_{i}>0$, $K_{i}\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and
$q^{K_{i}}\to0$.  With the “no completely missing SNV’’ ascertainment the
union $V$ is the set of sites with $p_{i}>0$ and

$$
E[S_{obs}]=\sum_{i\in V}\bigl[1-q^{K_{i}}\bigr]\longrightarrow
\sum_{i\in V}1=S_{true},
$$

i.e. $S_{obs}\xrightarrow{P} S_{true}$ on $V$.  Hence

$$
\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{p}
S_{true}/a_{n}=\hat\theta_{W}^{true}
$$

on the ascertained variant set.  Up to the $o(a_{n})$ loss of the
$k=O(1)$ tail the binary segregating/non-segregating information on
which $S/a_{n}$ is based is asymptotically preserved by random
genotype-independent deletion followed by reference imputation, whereas
the frequency information on which $\pi$ is based is permanently
$r$-shrunken.

That is the classic frequency-versus-presence robustness.  In the
textbook $n\to\infty$, $0<p_{i}<1$ idealisation $\hat\theta_{W}$ is
asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained VCF set and $\hat\pi$ is
systematically down biased by the reference imputation.  In strict
finite-$n$ expectation the $k=1,2,\dots$ tail gives a
$E[\Delta S]=\theta[-\log(1-q)]>0$ loss of $S$, i.e. a small practical
downward finite-sample bias for Watterson as well, with the relative
bias vanishing as $n\to\infty$; the $r$ attenuation of $\pi$ does not.

I agree with the B camp on the π part and I think that's the clearest part of the problem. Per-haplotype retention r<1 with deletion of a derived copy replaced by reference means X_i=Y_i R_i and E[p_obs]=r p < p. Then

E[diff_obs]=2pr[1-pr] < 2p(1-p)

site by site, so the average pairwise difference per ascertained site is permanently shrunk and π̂ is down biased for every n. That frequency attenuation does not go away.

The claim that Watterson is asymptotically preserved is the one I think needs qualification in the regime the problem describes. On the ascertained union V, a truly segregating site with k true derived copies is lost from S_obs iff all k copies are filtered in their own samples:

Pr{site lost | k}=q^k ,  q=1-r>0.

Hence

E[S_obs]= Σ_{i∈V}[1-q^{k_i}] < Σ_{i∈V}1 = S_true

in expectation for any finite panel. The q^{k}→0 argument is correct for a site with p_i fixed >0, i.e. k_i=2N p_i→∞. With an infinite-sites neutral spectrum that is not the relevant limit for the sum that defines θ̂_W.

Under infinite sites E[N_k]=θ/k. The expected loss of segregating sites is

E[ΔS]= Σ_{k≥1}θ/k q^k = θ[-log(1-q)]>0

and it is constant in N. The site-frequency spectrum is replenished as N grows: the number of k=1,2,… sites grows with the region, so the k=O(1) tail that dominates S in humans is always present. With a substantial minority filtered per sample q is a non-negligible constant, so Pr loss for a singleton is q, for a doubleton q², etc. Once the last carrier is filtered in its own sample the site is imputed to reference in every haplotype and becomes observationally monomorphic reference even though it is truly segregating in the VCF union.

The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition is a pre-filter property of the union panel. After independent per-sample deletion and reference imputation a site that is present in the union can be rendered monomorphic reference in the completed alignments. That is a genuine downward bias in the count of segregating sites and therefore in θ̂_W=S/a_n on the ascertained set V. The bias is small per common site and the relative loss vanishes like O(1/log n), but the absolute expected loss of rare sites is positive for every realistic, albeit arbitrarily large, sample.

So we have a systematic frequency shrinkage that biases π down and a systematic erasure of the last observed derived copy that biases S and hence Watterson’s estimator down. Reference imputation increases reference homozygosity at every site, it never creates derived alleles. Both the presence-only statistic and the frequency-weighted statistic are therefore systematically reduced relative to the true variation on the ascertained VCF set. In practice both θ̂_W and π̂ are downward biased by the random per-sample deletion plus reference imputation.

I agree with the core frequency-attenuation point for π and want to push the discussion on θW a bit further, because I think the asymptotic-presence argument is being used as an idealisation that does not match the estimator we actually compute on the imputed alignment.

On the union V of sites that enter the VCF let the per-haplotype retention probability be r<1, q=1−r>0. For a site with k true derived copies in the 2N panel the observed derived count after independent per-sample filtering and reference imputation is Binomial(k,r). The site is observed as segregating iff at least one copy survives

Pr{site survives | k}=1−q^{k} .

Hence

E[S_obs]= Σ_i [1−q^{k_i}] = S_true − Σ_i q^{k_i} < S_true

in expectation. The loss per site is q^{k}. For a fixed p>0, k=2Np→∞ and q^{k}→0, which is the fixed-p limit quoted for asymptotic preservation. The neutral site frequency spectrum is not a fixed-p set. With the infinite-sites model E[N_k]=θ/k for k=1,2,… and the expected number of sites erased by the filter+imputation is

E[ΔS]= Σ_{k≥1} θ/k q^{k}=θ[−log(1−q)]>0

for any substantial minority q>0. That mass comes from the k=O(1) tail that dominates S in humans. The condition “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ is a pre-filter ascertainment property; after independent per-sample deletion a true derived copy filtered in its own sample is written as reference in that haplotype. For a singleton the loss probability is q, for a doubleton q², etc. Those probabilities are constant in N, and the number of k=1,2,… sites grows with the sequenced region.

In other words, the observed allele count is stochastically ≤ the true count, so a site can become monomorphic reference in the imputed alignment even though it is truly segregating in the panel. That is a genuine downward bias in the number of segregating sites and therefore in θ̂W=S/a_n on the ascertained set V. The bias is small for common alleles where q^{k}≈0, but it is systematic for the rare-allele bulk that carries most of S and of θW in practice.

π is of course also deflated, site by site

E[p_obs|p]=pr<p,   E[diff_obs]=2pr[1−pr]<2p(1−p),

so pairwise differences are attenuated by the reference imputation for every segregating site that remains. The thinning p→pr is permanent and does not vanish with N.

Thus reference imputation both erodes the count of segregating sites that enters Watterson’s estimator and attenuates the allele frequencies that enter nucleotide diversity. In any realisable panel, and certainly for the arbitrarily large but finite panels we work with, both S_obs and π_obs are systematically lower than their true values on the ascertained VCF set. The textbook n→∞ fixed-p limit makes q^{k}→0 pointwise, but the integrated loss over the infinite-sites spectrum remains positive, so in practice both estimators are biased downward. That is the both-biased case.

I think the presence/absence vs frequency distinction being emphasized by the B camp is formally correct for a site with a *fixed* derived frequency p>0, but it does not describe what is actually summed when we compute θ_W and π from a real VCF panel.

On the ascertained union V we have per-haplotype retention r<1 and a deleted derived copy is imputed to reference. For a site with k true derived copies the probability it survives as segregating in the imputed alignment is 1−q^{k} with q=1−r, and the observed derived frequency is attenuated to p_obs≈r p in expectation. π is therefore down weighted site by site, 2pr[1−pr]<2p(1−p), and that frequency attenuation persists as n grows.

The same mechanism erodes S. The expected number of segregating sites that we actually count after imputation is

E[S_obs]=∑_{k≥1} E[N_k] [1−q^{k}] .

With the infinite-sites neutral spectrum E[N_k]=θ/k, so

E[S_obs]=θ∑_{k≥1}1/k − θ∑_{k≥1}q^{k}/k = S_true − θ[−log(1−q)]<S_true .

The loss term θ[−log(1−q)]>0 is a constant in n. For k=1,2,… the loss probability q^{k} is a non-negligible constant because the filter fraction is a substantial minority per sample, and the rare tail k=O(1) that dominates the human SFS is replenished as the panel grows. The condition “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ is a pre-filter property of the union panel; after independent per-sample deletion and reference imputation a truly segregating rare site becomes monomorphic reference whenever the few carriers that exist happen to be the samples in which that site is filtered out.

Hence E[S_obs]<S_true and E[θ̂_W,obs]=E[S_obs]/a_n<θ_W,true on the ascertained set V. As colleagues 13,14,16 and 17 note, q^{k}→0 pointwise for fixed p, but p is not fixed for the spectrum that enters the sum: the number of sites with bounded k grows with the region and the integrated absolute loss does not vanish.

We therefore get the classic reference imputation effect in both statistics: π is attenuated by p→pr, and the count of segregating sites that underlies Watterson’s estimator is systematically reduced by the non-zero probability of erasing the last observed derived copy of a rare site. In any realistic, arbitrarily large but finite panel both θ̂_W and π̂ computed from the completed alignments are downward biased relative to the true values on the ascertained SNV set. The asymptotic n→∞ limit used to claim asymptotic unbiasedness of S is an idealisation for fixed p>0 that is not compatible with the infinite-sites spectrum that actually generates S∼θ log n.

B. Only pi is biased, Watterson’s theta is asymptotically preserved on the ascertained VCF set.

Let r<1 be the per-haplotype retention probability after the random low-quality filter and q=1−r>0 the deletion probability. A deleted derived copy is imputed to reference, a reference copy is never changed. For a true derived frequency p>0

E[p_obs | p]=p r < p

and for two independent haplotypes

E[diff_obs | p]=2 p r[1−p r] < 2p(1−p)=E[diff_true | p]

for every 0<p<1. Hence on every ascertained site

π_i,obs = 2p_i^obs(1−p_i^obs) < 2p_i(1−p_i)=π_i,true

and after averaging over the union V of VCF sites

E[π̂_obs]=|V|^{-1}∑ 2r p_i[1−r p_i] < |V|^{-1}∑ 2p_i(1−p_i)=E[π̂_true].

Reference imputation turns a filtered derived copy into a reference match; the pairwise difference and hence nucleotide diversity is permanently attenuated by the constant factor r and the bias persists as n→∞.

Watterson’s statistic is presence/absence only, θ̂_W=S/a_n. A truly segregating site with k=2np true derived copies is lost from S only if all k copies are filtered in their own haplotypes,

Pr{S_i^obs=0 | p_i>0}=q^{k}=q^{2np_i}.

For any fixed p_i>0, k→∞ as n→∞ and q^{k}→0. With the stated “no completely missing SNV’’ condition the union V is the set of sites with p_i>0. Then

E[S_obs]=∑_{i∈V}[1−q^{k_i}] →∑_{i∈V}1=S_true

in probability, so S_obs→S_true and

θ̂_W,obs = S_obs/a_n → S_true/a_n = θ̂_W,true

on the ascertained variant set V. Up to the o(1) loss of the k=O(1) tail the binary segregating/non-segregating information that defines S is asymptotically preserved by random genotype-independent deletion followed by reference imputation. The frequency information on which π is based is not preserved.

That is the textbook frequency-vs-presence distinction. On the usual idealisation 0<p<1 on V, reference imputation gives a permanent downward bias of π and an asymptotically unbiased Watterson estimator on the ascertained set. The finite-n q^{k} loss for the very rarest singletons/doubletons is the source of the “both biased’’ finite-sample objection, but it vanishes relatively as the sample size is taken arbitrarily large, which is the limit invoked in the problem.

Hence in the large-n idealisation only nucleotide diversity is biased down; Watterson’s S/a_n is asymptotically robust to random per-sample deletion + reference imputation on the ascertained SNV set.

B. Only nucleotide diversity is biased down, Watterson’s $S/a_{n}$ is asymptotically preserved on the ascertained VCF set.

Let $V=U$ be the union of SNV positions that enter the VCFs, i.e. the set of sites with true derived frequency $p_{i}>0$ in the $2n$ phased haplotypes, and let $r<1$ be the per-haplotype retention probability for a true derived call. A deleted derived call is imputed to the reference allele, a reference allele is never changed. On a haplotype

$X_{i}=Y_{i}R_{i}$, $Y_{i}\sim {\rm Bern}(p_{i})$, $R_{i}\sim {\rm Bern}(r)$ independent,
$E[X_{i}]=rp_{i}<p_{i}$.

Hence for two independent haplotypes

$E[(X_{i}-X_{j})^{2}]=2rp_{i}\bigl[1-rp_{i}\bigr]<2p_{i}(1-p_{i})$

for every $0<p_{i}<1$.  On every truly segregating ascertained site

$\pi_{i}^{obs}=2p_{i}^{obs}\!\left(1-p_{i}^{obs}\right)
<2p_{i}(1-p_{i})=\pi_{i}^{true},$

and averaging over $V$

$E[\hat\pi_{obs}]=|V|^{-1}\sum_{i}2rp_{i}[1-rp_{i}]
<|V|^{-1}\sum_{i}2p_{i}(1-p_{i})=E[\hat\pi_{true}]$.

Reference imputation turns every filtered derived copy into a reference match, so the observed pairwise differences are permanently down-weighted by the $p\to rp$ attenuation. In the rare-variant regime $p_{i}\ll1$, $E[\pi_{obs}]\approx rE[\pi_{true}]$. The bias does not vanish with $n$.

Presence/absence is different. For a truly segregating site with $k_{i}=2np_{i}>0$ true derived copies

$\Pr\{p_{i}^{obs}=0\mid p_{i}>0\}=q^{k_{i}},\qquad q=1-r,$

i.e. the site is lost from $S$ only if all $k_{i}$ copies are filtered in their own haplotypes. For any fixed $p_{i}>0$, $k_{i}\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and $q^{k_{i}}\to0$. With the stated “no completely missing SNV’’ ascertainment

$E[S_{obs}]=\sum_{i\in V}\bigl[1-q^{k_{i}}\bigr]\to\sum_{i\in V}1=S_{true}$

in probability, so $S_{obs}=S_{true}+o_{p}(a_{n})$ and

$\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}\xrightarrow{p}S_{true}/a_{n}
=\hat\theta_{W}^{true}$

on the ascertained variant set $V$. The binary segregating/non-segregating information on which Watterson’s estimator is based is asymptotically retained by random genotype-independent deletion followed by reference imputation, whereas the frequency information on which $\pi$ is based is permanently attenuated.

Up to the conventional $o(1)$ loss of the $k=O(1)$ tail, which is $O(1)$ against $E[S]\sim\theta\log n$, this is the textbook reference-imputation bias: $\pi$ is systematically downward biased, $\hat\theta_{W}=S/a_{n}$ is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained SNV set. The usual genome-wide per-base ascertainment inflation applies to both estimators, but the frequency-dependent reference-imputation effect is a down bias of $\pi$ with an essentially intact Watterson $S/a_{n}$ in the $n\to\infty$ idealisation stated in the problem. Finite-$n$ the $k=1,2,\dots$ tail gives a small $O(1)$ absolute downward loss of $S$, the conventional “both biased in finite samples’’ caveat.

I think the asymptotic presence/absence argument being used for θW is being taken at face value in a way that does not match the site-frequency spectrum we actually sum over.

Yes, for a site with a fixed derived frequency p>0, k=2Np→∞ with N and Pr{site lost}=q^{k}→0. That is the math that supports B. The problem, however, is not a fixed set of sites with fixed p>0. The panel is ascertained on the union V of SNVs that are segregating in the panel, and under the infinite-sites model the number of sites with k derived copies is E[N_k]=θ/k. As N grows the spectrum replenishes: new singletons, doubletons, etc. are continually created at frequency O(1/N). For those k=O(1) classes q^{k} is a constant >0.

With per-haplotype retention r<1 and loss q=1-r>0, conditioned on the k true derived copies the site is still seen as segregating after per-sample filtering + reference imputation iff at least one copy survives:

Pr{survive|k}=1−q^{k}.

Hence
E[S_obs]= Σ_{k≥1} E[N_k][1−q^{k}]
       = θ Σ_{k≥1}1/k − θ Σ_{k≥1}q^{k}/k
       = S_true − θ[−log(1−q)] < S_true.

The loss θ[−log(1−q)]>0 does not vanish with N. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition only guarantees the site is in the union panel V before filtering; it does not guarantee a derived copy survives imputation in the samples that carry it. A true derived allele that is filtered in the only sample that carries it is imputed to reference in that haplotype, and if all k carriers are hit by the sample-specific filter the site becomes monomorphic reference in the reconstructed alignment.

That is the same asymmetry that biases π. Observed derived frequency is p_obs = r p in expectation, so E[diff_obs]=2rp[1−rp] < 2p(1−p) site by site, and reference imputation turns every filtered derived copy into a reference match. π is therefore systematically deflated and the deflation persists for all N.

Both statistics are functions of the imputed alignment. π is attenuated by the within-site frequency shrinkage p→rp, and S, and hence θW=S/a_n, is attenuated by the non-zero probability q^{k}>0 of erasing the last observed copy of a rare site. The rare tail k=1,2,… dominates S in humans, and with a substantial minority filtered per sample q is a non-negligible constant. The relative bias in S/a_n vanishes as log N grows, but the absolute expected loss of segregating sites remains positive for any realisable, arbitrarily large but finite panel.

In practice we therefore get a downward bias in the number of segregating sites that enters Watterson’s estimator and an additional downward frequency bias in pairwise differences. Both θ̂_W and π̂ computed from the completed sequences are systematically biased low relative to the true values on the ascertained SNV set.

I think the π downward bias is clear and uncontroversial, and the θW issue is where the disagreement is. Conceding the frequency attenuation is enough for π: on a haplotype X = Y R with retention probability r<1, E[p_obs]=r p and E[diff_obs]=2 r p[1−r p] <2 p(1−p) site by site, so pairwise differences are permanently thinned by reference imputation of the filtered derived copies. That bias survives n→∞.

The same per-sample deletion mechanism also erodes the segregating-site count that θW is built on. A truly segregating ascertained site with k true derived copies in the 2N panel is observed as segregating only if at least one of those k copies survives in its own sample. With per-haplotype loss probability q>0,

Pr{ site lost | k } = q^{k},
E[S_obs]=∑_{k≥1} N_k [1−q^{k}] .

For a fixed p>0, k=2 N p→∞ and q^{k}→0, which is the fixed-p asymptotic argument used for the “asymptotically unbiased” claim for S. The site-frequency spectrum used in practice is not a fixed-p set. Under infinite sites E[N_k]=θ/k for k=1,2,…, so the expected absolute loss of segregating sites is

E[ΔS]=∑_{k≥1} θ/k q^{k}=θ[−log(1−q)]>0,

independent of N. It is positive as soon as a substantial minority of calls is filtered per sample, q>0. The number of sites with bounded k grows with the panel, so the rare tail that dominates S in humans is never emptied by increasing N: a singleton is lost with probability q, a doubleton with q², etc. 

The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition only guarantees the site is in the union V before filtering; after independent per-sample deletion and reference imputation a site can become monomorphic reference in the reconstructed alignments whenever the few carriers that exist in the panel happen to be the samples in which that site is filtered out. The imputation is not missing at random with respect to allele state – a true derived allele can only be turned into reference, never created – so the observed allele count is stochastically ≤ the true count.

Hence E[S_obs] < S_true in expectation for any feasible sample size and θ̂_W,obs = S_obs/a_n is downward biased on the ascertained VCF set, in addition to the frequency attenuation that biases π. The q^{k}→0 limit holds pointwise for a site with p fixed >0, but the integrated loss over the replenishing rare-allele spectrum remains >0. Under the realistic human SFS both a presence-only statistic and a frequency-weighted statistic are systematically reduced by random per-sample deletion followed by reference imputation.

That is the usual operational statement: reference imputation both erodes the count of segregating sites and attenuates allele frequencies, giving downward bias for both θW and π on the data that are actually computed.

Let r<1 be the per-haplotype retention probability and q=1-r>0 the per-haplotype deletion probability. For a haplotype X = Y R with Y the true derived indicator and R the retention indicator, E[X]=r p < p. For two independent haplotypes

E[diff_obs|p]=2 pr[1-pr] < 2p(1-p)

for every 0<p<1, and the inequality is strict site by site. A filtered derived copy is forced to reference, so every pair that is truly different is scored as identical whenever one or both members lose the call. Averaged over the ascertained VCF set V the observed pairwise differences are therefore permanently attenuated, E[π_obs] < π_true, with the usual rare-allele approximation E[π_obs]≈r E[π_true]. That frequency-dependent shrinkage survives n→∞.

The presence/absence argument for Watterson is the point of contention. For a site with k true derived copies in the 2N panel the site is rendered monomorphic reference after imputation iff all k copies are filtered in their own samples,

Pr{site lost | k}= q^{k} >0

so that

E[S_obs]= Σ_{k≥1} E[N_k] [1 - q^{k}].

On the ascertained set V the condition “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ only guarantees the site is in the union panel, it does not guarantee a derived copy survives imputation in the samples that carry it.

On the neutral infinite-sites spectrum E[N_k]=θ/k. Hence the expected absolute loss of segregating sites is

E[ΔS]= Σ_{k≥1} θ/k q^{k}= θ [-log(1-q)] >0

for any q>0. The loss probability goes to zero for a fixed p>0 because k=2Np→∞, but the spectrum is not fixed as N grows. The number of sites with k=1,2,… is O(θ) for all N and it is exactly the rare tail that dominates S in humans. For a singleton the loss probability is q, for a doubleton q^{2}, etc., with q a substantial minority per sample. The per-site loss →0 for common alleles, but the integrated loss over the replenishing rare-allele tail remains positive and does not vanish in expectation.

Therefore E[S_obs] < S_true on the ascertained VCF set and

E[θ̂_W,obs]=E[S_obs]/a_n < S_true/a_n

is downward biased. The textbook q^{k}→0 statement is a pointwise limit for fixed p>0. It is not uniform over the infinite-sites spectrum, which supplies an ever-growing number of sites with k=O(1) as N→∞. In practice, with a constant per-sample filter rate and reference imputation, both the count of segregating sites that enters Watterson’s estimator and the frequency-weighted pairwise differences that define nucleotide diversity are systematically reduced. The reference-imputation step is not neutral for the site frequency spectrum and it leaves a systematic downward shift in both the count of segregating sites and the frequency-weighted pairwise differences.

Write r<1 for the per-haplotype retention probability and q=1−r>0 for the per-sample deletion probability. On a haplotype the observed derived indicator is X = Y R with Y the true derived indicator and R the retention indicator, so E[X|Y=1]=r and E[p_obs|p]=r p < p for every 0<p<1. Hence for two independent haplotypes

E[diff_obs|p]=2 r p [1−r p] < 2 p (1−p)=E[diff_true|p]

and averaging over the ascertained VCF set V

E[π̂_obs]=|V|^{-1} Σ 2 r p_i[1−r p_i] < |V|^{-1} Σ 2 p_i(1−p_i)=π_true.

Every filtered derived copy is written as reference, so pairwise differences are under-counted at every segregating site. That is the permanent frequency-attenuation effect on π.

The same thinning hits S. A truly segregating site with k≥1 true derived copies in the 2N panel is observed as segregating iff at least one copy survives its own sample. Conditional on k

Pr{site survives|k}=1−q^{k},   Pr{site lost|k}=q^{k}>0.

Hence

E[S_obs]= Σ_{k≥1} E[N_k][1−q^{k}] < Σ_{k≥1} E[N_k]=S_true.

Under the infinite-sites model E[N_k]=θ/k, so the expected absolute loss is

E[ΔS]=θ Σ_{k≥1} q^{k}/k = θ[−log(1−q)]>0

for any q>0. The loss probability q^{k} goes to zero for a site with fixed p>0 as k=2Np→∞, but the SFS continually replenishes the k=O(1) tail as N grows. Singletons are lost with probability q, doubletons with q², etc., and the number of sites with bounded k grows with the sequenced region. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition refers to ascertainment of the union panel V before filtering; after independent per-sample deletion and reference imputation a site that is truly segregating in V can become monomorphic reference in the reconstructed alignments when the few carriers in the panel are precisely the samples in which the site is filtered out.

Thus E[S_obs] < S_true in expectation for any realistic, arbitrarily large but finite panel and θ̂_W,obs=S_obs/a_n is downward biased on the ascertained set V. The bias is largest for the rare-allele bulk that dominates S in humans.

Reference imputation therefore removes variation both from the presence/absence count that underlies Watterson’s estimator and from the frequency-weighted average that defines nucleotide diversity. Both θ̂_W and π̂ computed from the completed alignments are systematically biased low relative to the true values on the ascertained SNV set, with π̂ additionally attenuated by the p→r p frequency shrinkage.

That is the expected downward bias for both statistics under random per-sample deletion followed by reference imputation.

The data that are analysed are the union

$V=\{s:s\;{\rm is\;in\;at\;least\;one\;VCF}\}$

and, after quality filtering, a true derived copy is kept on a

haplotypes.  A filtered derived copy is written as reference.  Write
$Y_{i}\in\{0,1\}$ for the true derived indicator and $R_{i}\in\{0,1\}$
for retention, $Y_{i}\perp R_{i}$, $E[R_{i}]=r$.  On a haplotype

$E[\,p_{obs}\mid p\,]=rp<p$

and for two independent haplotypes

$E[\,{\rm diff}_{obs}\mid p\,]=2rp\,[1-rp]<2p(1-p)=
E[\,{\rm diff}_{true}\mid p\,]$

for every $0<p<1$.  Hence on every ascertained site

$\pi_{i}^{\rm obs}=2p_{i}^{obs}\!\left(1-p_{i}^{obs}\right)
<2p_{i}(1-p_{i})=\pi_{i}^{true}$

and averaging over $V$

$E[\hat\pi_{obs}]
 =|V|^{-1}\sum_{i}2rp_{i}\!\left[1-rp_{i}\right]
 <|V|^{-1}\sum_{i}2p_{i}(1-p_{i})=E[\hat\pi_{true}]$,

with $E[\pi_{obs}]\simeq rE[\pi_{true}]$ in the rare-allele regime.

$p\mapsto rp$.  The downward attenuation persists for all $n$, in

Presence/absence is a different statistic.  Watterson uses

$\hat\theta_{W}=S/a_{n},\qquad S=\sum_{i}{\bf1}\{p_{i}^{obs}>0\}$.

of true derived copies in the $2n$ phased haplotypes.  The site is lost
from $S$ only if all $K_{i}$ copies are filtered in their own samples,

$\Pr\{p_{i}^{obs}=0\mid p_{i}>0\}=q^{K_{i}}=q^{2np_{i}}$.

For any fixed $p_{i}>0$, $K_{i}\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and
$q^{K_{i}}\to0$.  With the “no completely missing SNV’’ ascertainment
every site in $V$ has $p_{i}>0$ and

$E[S_{obs}]=\sum_{i\in V}\!\left[1-q^{K_{i}}\right]
\to\sum_{i\in V}1=S_{true}$

in probability, i.e.

$S_{obs}\xrightarrow{P}S_{true},\qquad
\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}\xrightarrow{P}
S_{true}/a_{n}=\hat\theta_{W}^{true}$

on the ascertained variant set $V$.  The binary segregating/non-
segregating information on which $\theta_{W}=S/a_{n}$ is based is
asymptotically preserved by random, genotype-independent deletion
followed by reference imputation, whereas the frequency information on
which $\pi$ is based is permanently thinned by the $p\to rp$

On the union $V$ of sites that enter the VCF let $p_{i}>0$ be the true
derived frequency in the $2n$ phased haplotypes and let $r<1$ be the
per-haplotype retention probability after the random low-quality filter.
A deleted derived copy is written as reference, so on a haplotype

$$
X_{i}=Y_{i}R_{i},\qquad E[X_{i}\mid Y_{i}=1]=r,
$$

and with $Y_{i}\perp R_{i}$

$$
E[p_{i}^{obs}\mid p_{i}]=r p_{i}<p_{i},\qquad 0<p_{i}<1 .
$$

Hence for two independent haplotypes

$$
E\big[(X_{i}-X_{j})^{2}\mid p_{i}\big]=2pr\bigl[1-pr\bigr]
   <2p(1-p)=E\big[(Y_{i}-Y_{j})^{2}\mid p_{i}\big]
$$

site by site.  The observed heterozygosity is therefore

$$
\pi_{i}^{obs}=2p_{i}^{obs}\bigl(1-p_{i}^{obs}\bigr)
     <2p_{i}(1-p_{i})=\pi_{i}^{true},\qquad 0<p_{i}<1,
$$

and on the ascertained set

$$
\hat \pi_{obs}=|V|^{-1}\sum_{i\in V}2\hat p_{i}^{obs}
\bigl(1-\hat p_{i}^{obs}\bigr)
<|V|^{-1}\sum_{i\in V}2p_{i}(1-p_{i}) .
$$

The $p\to pr$ thinning is a constant frequency-dependent attenuation.
In the rare allele regime $p_{i}\ll1$, $E[\pi_{i}^{obs}]\simeq r\,
E[\pi_{i}^{true}]$, and the down shift persists for every $n$ and for
$n\to\infty$.  Reference imputation turns every filtered derived copy
into a reference match, so pairwise differences are systematically
under-counted.  $\pi$ is frequency weighted and is permanently deflated
by the reference imputation.

Presence/absence is different.  Let $K_{i}=2np_{i}$ be the true number of
derived copies at $i$.  The site is lost from the segregating-site count
iff all $K_{i}$ copies are filtered in their own samples,

$$
\Pr\{p_{i}^{obs}=0\mid p_{i}>0\}=q^{K_{i}},\qquad q=1-r .
$$

For any fixed $p_{i}>0$, $K_{i}\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and
$q^{K_{i}}\to0$.  With the “no completely missing SNV’’ ascertainment the
union $V$ is the set of sites with $p_{i}>0$ and

$$
E[S_{obs}]=\sum_{i\in V}\bigl[1-q^{K_{i}}\bigr]\longrightarrow
\sum_{i\in V}1=S_{true},
$$

i.e. $S_{obs}\xrightarrow{P} S_{true}$ on $V$.  Hence

$$
\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{p}
S_{true}/a_{n}=\hat\theta_{W}^{true}
$$

on the ascertained variant set.  Up to the $o(a_{n})$ loss of the
$k=O(1)$ tail the binary segregating/non-segregating information on
which $S/a_{n}$ is based is asymptotically preserved by random
genotype-independent deletion followed by reference imputation, whereas
the frequency information on which $\pi$ is based is permanently
$r$-shrunken.

That is the classic frequency-versus-presence robustness.  In the
textbook $n\to\infty$, $0<p_{i}<1$ idealisation $\hat\theta_{W}$ is
asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained VCF set and $\hat\pi$ is
systematically down biased by the reference imputation.  In strict
finite-$n$ expectation the $k=1,2,\dots$ tail gives a
$E[\Delta S]=\theta[-\log(1-q)]>0$ loss of $S$, i.e. a small practical
downward finite-sample bias for Watterson as well, with the relative
bias vanishing as $n\to\infty$; the $r$ attenuation of $\pi$ does not.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core mechanism is unchanged from earlier rounds. Per-haplotype retention r<1, loss q=1-r>0, deleted derived copies imputed to reference. For a true derived frequency p>0,
E[p_obs]=r p < p,
E[diff_obs|p]=2 r p[1-r p] < 2p(1-p)
site by site. Hence nucleotide diversity is permanently frequency-attenuated on the ascertained VCF union V, E[π_obs]≈ r E[π_true] in the rare-allele regime, bias persists for all n and n→∞. This π downward bias is uncontested; colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,6,8,B-camp and 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,C-camp all agree.

Watterson is the split point. Presence/absence only:
θ_W = S/a_n, S = Σ 1{p_obs>0}.
For a site with k=2np true derived copies,
Pr{site lost|k}=q^k, Pr{site survives}=1-q^k.
For fixed p>0, k→∞ with n and q^k→0, so pointwise S_obs→S_true in probability on V. That yields the textbook large-n claim:
E[S_obs]= Σ[1-q^{k_i}]→ Σ1, S_obs→S_true, θ_W^obs→θ_W^true on V,
i.e. the binary segregating/non-segregating information is asymptotically preserved by genotype-independent random deletion + reference imputation, while frequency info is not. This is the B only-π-biased statement championed by colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,6,8.

The C camp stresses the infinite-sites spectrum and integrated expectation. Under infinite sites E[N_k]=θ/k. Expected absolute loss of segregating sites on V is
E[ΔS]= Σ θ/k q^k = θ[-log(1-q)]>0,
independent of n. The loss comes from the k=O(1) tail, singletons lost with prob q, doubletons q², etc. The number of k=O(1) sites is replenished as n grows, so the absolute expected loss does not vanish; E[S_obs]<S_true in expectation for any finite panel, and θ_W is downward biased in absolute terms. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition is a pre-filter ascertainment of V; after independent per-sample deletion a site can become monomorphic reference in the imputed alignment when all k carriers are filtered in their own samples. Pointwise q^k→0 for fixed p is not uniform over the spectrum. Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7 argue this operational regime makes both θ_W and π biased down.

Additional nuance: strict set-theoretic V may contain fixed-derived sites f=1 w.r.t. reference. Reference imputation then creates artefactual polymorphism, Pr{segregating|f=1}→1, giving an upward contribution to S and π that competes with the downward attenuation on 0<f<1. Under the conventional idealisation S_{f=1}=0 this upward effect is absent, noted by colleague 4.

Ascertainment to variable sites V also inflates both estimators per base relative to whole-genome expectation; the reference-imputation effect per ascertained site is the π down bias described above.

Current synthesis: textbook arbitrarily-large-sample idealisation intended by the problem statement is the frequency-vs-presence robustness: π is persistently down-biased by p→rp attenuation, Watterson’s S/a_n is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained SNV set V, i.e. B. Finite-n/absolute-expectation reading gives both statistics downward biased because E[ΔS]=θ[-log(1-q)]>0, i.e. C, with π also suffering within-site frequency shrinkage. The disagreement is precisely asymptotic relative bias of S/a_n vanishing as a_n~log n vs positive integrated absolute loss of rare sites. The problem phrasing “number of samples is arbitrarily large’’ points to the asymptotic B reading, with the finite-n both-biased caveat retained.

With the “no completely missing SNV” condition the union V is the set of sites with p>0, so E[S_obs]=∑[1-q^{k_i}]→∑1=S_true in probability and S_obs→S_true. On the ascertained variant set V, θ̂_W is asymptotically unbiased in the textbook n→∞ fixed-p idealisation. The binary segregating/non-segregating information is asymptotically preserved whereas the frequency information is permanently r-shrunk. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8 enforce this B-camp position: only π is biased, θ̂_W is asymptotically robust on V.

The disagreement is about the integrated site-frequency spectrum. Under infinite sites E[N_k]=θ/k. The expected absolute loss of segregating sites is E[ΔS]=∑ θ/k q^k = θ[-log(1-q)]>0, constant in n. For singletons loss prob = q, doubletons q², etc. The “no completely missing SNV” condition is pre-filter ascertainment; after independent per-sample deletion a site can become monomorphic reference in the imputed alignment when the few carriers that exist are exactly the samples in which the site is filtered. Hence in expectation E[S_obs] < S_true for any finite although arbitrarily large panel, so E[θ̂_W] < θ_W,true. The q^k→0 limit holds pointwise for fixed p>0 but not uniformly over the replenishing rare-allele tail that dominates S in humans. Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7 argue this C-camp position: both θ̂_W and π are downward biased in expectation, with π additionally suffering within-site frequency shrinkage.

Additional nuance: the VCF union contains sites fixed derived relative to reference, f=1. Under imputation such a site becomes spuriously segregating with expected heterozygosity 2r(1-r)>0, so S can be inflated by f=1 sites while π is still deflated on 0<f<1 sites. The textbook asymptotic unbiasedness of θ_W is the 0<f<1 idealisation.

Current understanding: π is unambiguously downward biased by reference imputation. θ_W is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained VCF set in the n→∞ fixed-p idealisation that the problem statement invites with “number of samples is arbitrarily large”. Realistically with a constant per-sample filter rate and an infinite-sites spectrum the expected number of rare segregating sites erased is θ[-log(1-q)]>0, giving a practical downward bias in S and θ_W; the relative bias vanishes as S∼θ log n but does not vanish in expectation. E[S_obs]= Σ[1-q^{k_i}]→ Σ1, S_obs→S_true, θ_W^obs→θ_W^true on V,
i.e. the binary segregating/non-segregating information is asymptotically preserved by genotype-independent random deletion + reference imputation, while frequency info is not. This is the B only-π-biased statement championed by colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,6,8.

The C camp stresses the infinite-sites spectrum and integrated expectation. Under infinite sites E[N_k]=θ/k. Expected absolute loss of segregating sites on V is
E[ΔS]= Σ θ/k q^k = θ[-log(1-q)]>0,
independent of n. The loss comes from the k=O(1) tail, singletons lost with prob q, doubletons q², etc. The number of k=O(1) sites is replenished as n grows, so the absolute expected loss does not vanish; E[S_obs]<S_true in expectation for any finite panel, and θ_W is downward biased in absolute terms. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition is a pre-filter ascertainment of V; after independent per-sample deletion a site can become monomorphic reference in the imputed alignment when all k carriers are filtered in their own samples. Pointwise q^k→0 for fixed p is not uniform over the spectrum. Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7 argue this operational regime makes both θ_W and π biased down.

Additional nuance: strict set-theoretic V may contain fixed-derived sites f=1 w.r.t. reference. Reference imputation then creates artefactual polymorphism, Pr{segregating|f=1}→1, giving an upward contribution to S and π that competes with the downward attenuation on 0<f<1. Under the conventional idealisation S_{f=1}=0 this upward effect is absent, noted by colleague 4.

Ascertainment to variable sites V also inflates both estimators per base relative to whole-genome expectation; the reference-imputation effect per ascertained site is the π down bias described above.

Current synthesis: textbook arbitrarily-large-sample idealisation intended by the problem statement is the frequency-vs-presence robustness: π is persistently down-biased by p→rp attenuation, Watterson’s S/a_n is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained SNV set V, i.e. B. Finite-n/absolute-expectation reading gives both statistics downward biased because E[ΔS]=θ[-log(1-q)]>0, i.e. C, with π also suffering within-site frequency shrinkage. The disagreement is precisely asymptotic relative bias of S/a_n vanishing as a_n~log n vs positive integrated absolute loss of rare sites. The problem phrasing “number of samples is arbitrarily large’’ points to the asymptotic B reading, with the finite-n both-biased caveat retained.
reflection_text.15:
The union of positions that enters the analysis is V, the set of SNV positions that are present in at least one VCF. After quality filtering a true derived allele is retained per haplotype with probability r=1-q<1 independent across haplotypes, and every deleted call is imputed to reference. For a true derived frequency p>0

E[p_obs|p]=p r < p

and for a pair

E[diff_obs|p]=2pr(1-pr) < 2p(1-p)=E[diff_true|p].

Pairwise nucleotide diversity is a frequency weighted average of 2p(1-p). Reference imputation therefore systematically attenuates allele frequencies and depresses pairwise differences at every segregating site. The bias persists as n→∞ because pr < p for all p>0; in the rare-allele regime E[π_obs]≈r E[π_true].

Watterson’s estimator is θ_W=S/a_n with S the number of sites with p_obs>0. A truly segregating site with k=2np true derived copies is lost from S only if every copy is filtered: Pr{S_i^obs=0|p_i>0}=q^{k}=q^{2np_i}. For any fixed p_i>0, k→∞ as n→∞ so q^{k}→0. With the “no completely missing SNV’’ condition the set V is the set of sites with p_i>0. Then E[S_obs]=∑[1-q^{k_i}]→∑1=S_true in probability and θ_W^obs→θ_W^true on V. Presence/absence of a polymorphism is asymptotically preserved by random per-sample deletion + reference imputation; only the frequency information needed for π is thinned.

The disagreement in the round is the finite-sample / infinite-sites caveat. With a constant per-sample filter rate q>0 the expected loss of the rare tail is

E[ΔS]=∑_{k≥1} θ/k q^{k}=θ[-log(1-q)]>0

in the infinite-sites model, so E[S_obs]<S_true for any finite N and the loss is driven by singletons/doubletons whose k stays O(1) as N grows. Several colleagues therefore argue for a practical downward bias of θ_W as well, i.e. C both biased. In the textbook N→∞ idealisation with p fixed per site the loss probability per site vanishes and the dominant persistent effect is the downward bias of π while θ_W is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained SNV set, i.e. answer B, with the finite-n rare-allele loss being the caveat that pushes the practical view toward C.

Current belief: under the stated “arbitrarily large’’ sample idealisation and on the ascertained VCF set V, π is systematically down-biased by the p→pr attenuation whereas θ_W=S/a_n is asymptotically unbiased, the classic frequency-vs-presence robustness. The finite-sample infinite-sites integrated loss E[ΔS]>0 is the acknowledged reason the C camp argues both estimators are biased down in practice. Unresolved is whether the problem intends the strict n→∞ pointwise limit, giving B only π biased, or the operational infinite-sites expectation giving C both biased.

reflection_text.18:
The per-haplotype random deletion + reference imputation is genotype-dependent thinning. Let retention per haplotype be r=1-q<1. With true derived indicator Y and retention R independent, imputed indicator X=Y R. Then E[p_obs]=r p < p and for two independent haplotypes E[diff_obs|p]=2 r p[1-r p] < 2p(1-p) for 0<p<1. Hence site by site π_i^obs =2 p_i^obs(1-p_i^obs) < 2p_i(1-p_i). Averaged over the VCF union V the observed nucleotide diversity is permanently down-weighted, ≈r in the rare-allele regime p<<1. This attenuation persists for all n and as n→∞. π is uncontroversially downward biased by reference imputation.

Watterson’s estimator uses presence/absence only, θ̂_W=S/a_n. A truly segregating ascertained site with k=2 n p true derived copies is lost from S iff all k copies are filtered in their own samples: Pr{loss|k}=q^k. For any fixed p>0, k→∞ as n→∞ and q^k→0. With the “no completely missing SNV” condition the union V is the set of sites with p>0, so E[S_obs]=∑[1-q^{k_i}]→∑1=S_true in probability and S_obs→S_true. On the ascertained variant set V, θ̂_W is asymptotically unbiased in the textbook n→∞ fixed-p idealisation. The binary segregating/non-segregating information is asymptotically preserved whereas the frequency information is permanently r-shrunk. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8 enforce this B-camp position: only π is biased, θ̂_W is asymptotically robust on V.

The disagreement is about the integrated site-frequency spectrum. Under infinite sites E[N_k]=θ/k. The expected absolute loss of segregating sites is E[ΔS]=∑ θ/k q^k = θ[-log(1-q)]>0, constant in n. For singletons loss prob = q, doubletons q², etc. The “no completely missing SNV” condition is pre-filter ascertainment; after independent per-sample deletion a site can become monomorphic reference in the imputed alignment when the few carriers that exist are exactly the samples in which the site is filtered. Hence in expectation E[S_obs] < S_true for any finite although arbitrarily large panel, so E[θ̂_W] < θ_W,true. The q^k→0 limit holds pointwise for fixed p>0 but not uniformly over the replenishing rare-allele tail that dominates S in humans. Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7 argue this C-camp position: both θ̂_W and π are downward biased in expectation, with π additionally suffering within-site frequency shrinkage.

Additional nuance: the VCF union contains sites fixed derived relative to reference, f=1. Under imputation such a site becomes spuriously segregating with expected heterozygosity 2r(1-r)>0, so S can be inflated by f=1 sites while π is still deflated on 0<f<1 sites. The textbook asymptotic unbiasedness of θ_W is the 0<f<1 idealisation.

Current understanding: π is unambiguously downward biased by reference imputation. θ_W is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained VCF set in the n→∞ fixed-p idealisation that the problem statement invites with “number of samples is arbitrarily large”. Realistically with a constant per-sample filter rate and an infinite-sites spectrum the expected number of rare segregating sites erased is θ[-log(1-q)]>0, giving a practical downward bias in S and θ_W; the relative bias vanishes as S∼θ log n but does not vanish in expectation. Unresolved is how the question intends the f=1 fixed-derived artefact and the per-base vs per-variable-site normalisation to be handled.

On a haplotype X = Y R, Y~Bern(p), R~Bern(r) independent, E[X]=pr < p, observed derived frequency is attenuated p_obs = pr.

Pr{site lost | p>0}=q^k, q=1-r.

That is a constant absolute downward bias for S, and hence for θ_W, driven by the rare k=1,2,… tail that is constantly replenished as n grows. large’’ $\pi$ is systematically down-biased by the $p\to rp$ attenuation and
$\hat\theta_W=S/a_n$ is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained SNV set
$V$. The finite-$n$ $q^k$ loss of the $k=O(1)$ tail gives a small $O(1)$

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The π part is settled and I think everyone agrees on it. The panel is ascertained on the union V of sites with p>0. Conditioned on k true derived copies in 2N, the site is still seen as segregating after independent per-sample filtering + reference imputation iff at least one copy survives, Pr{survive|k}=1−q^{k}. Hence

E[ΔS]=θ∑_{k≥1} q^{k}/k = θ[−log(1−q)]>0

for any q>0. The loss mass comes from the k=O(1) tail. After independent per-sample deletion a carrier can be precisely the haplotype in which the site is filtered out, and the imputed alignment then has the site as reference in every haplotype. Reference imputation is non-MAR with respect to allele state: a true derived copy can only be turned into reference, never created. So the observed allele count is stochastically ≤ the true count and a truly segregating site can become observationally monomorphic reference.

That is the same asymmetry that biases π: reference imputation increases reference homozygosity at every site. The π part is settled and I think everyone agrees on it. With retention r<1 on a haplotype X=Y R we have E[p_obs]=r p and E[diff_obs]=2rp[1-rp] < 2p(1-p) site by site, so reference imputation turns every filtered derived copy into a reference match and nucleotide diversity is permanently attenuated p→rp. That bias does not vanish with n.

Where the disagreement lies is the interpretation of the q^{k}→0 argument for Watterson. For a site with fixed p>0, k=2np→∞ and Pr{site lost|k}=q^{k}→0, so pointwise the presence/absence information is asymptotically preserved. That is correct mathematically, but it is not the limit we actually sum over when we compute S/a_n on a VCF panel.

The panel is ascertained on the union V of sites with p>0. Conditioned on k true derived copies in 2N, the site is still seen as segregating after independent per-sample filtering + reference imputation iff at least one copy survives, Pr{survive|k}=1−q^{k}. Hence

E[S_obs]=∑_i[1−q^{k_i}] = ∑_k E[N_k][1−q^{k}].

Under infinite sites E[N_k]=θ/k and the expected absolute loss on the ascertained set is

E[ΔS]=θ∑_{k≥1} q^{k}/k = θ[−log(1−q)]>0

for any q>0. The loss mass comes from the k=O(1) tail. The number of singletons, doubletons and so on is replenished as N grows, so the k=1,2,… classes that dominate S in humans are never emptied by increasing N. For a singleton the loss probability is q, for a doubleton q², etc. With a substantial minority filtered per sample q is a non-negligible constant.

The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition fixes the union V before filtering. After independent per-sample deletion a carrier can be precisely the haplotype in which the site is filtered out, and the imputed alignment then has the site as reference in every haplotype. Reference imputation is non-MAR with respect to allele state: a true derived copy can only be turned into reference, never created. So the observed allele count is stochastically ≤ the true count and a truly segregating site can become observationally monomorphic reference.

That is the same asymmetry that biases π: reference imputation increases reference homozygosity at every site. It both attenuates allele frequencies within sites that remain segregating and erases the last observed derived copy of rare sites. Colleagues 13,14,16,17 and 2,5,7,9 have already highlighted that q^{k}→0 holds pointwise for fixed p>0 but the integrated loss over the replenishing rare-allele spectrum remains positive.

Hence E[p_obs|p]=r p < p and for two independent haplotypes E[diff_obs|p]=2 r p[1 - r p] < 2 p(1-p). Site by site π_i^obs=2 p_i^obs(1-p_i^obs) < 2 p_i(1-p_i). Reference imputation turns every filtered derived copy into a reference match, i.e. a permanent p→r p attenuation. In the rare regime E[π_obs]≈r E[π_true] and the downward shift persists for all n and as n→∞. Nucleotide diversity is frequency weighted and is permanently deflated.

Watterson uses presence/absence: θ̂_W=S/a_n, S=∑1{p_obs>0}. For a site with k=2 n p true derived copies Pr{site lost|k}=q^k, Pr{survive|k}=1-q^k. With fixed p>0, k→∞ as n→∞ and q^k→0, so pointwise S_obs→S_true on the ascertained union V of sites with p>0 and θ̂_W^obs→P S_true/a_n. The binary segregating/non-segregating information is asymptotically preserved by genotype-independent random deletion + reference imputation, whereas frequency information is permanently r-shrunk.

The disagreement is about the sum over the site-frequency spectrum. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,6,8 argue the textbook large-n idealisation: on the ascertained VCF set V, S_obs→P S_true, so θ̂_W is asymptotically unbiased and only π is biased, i.e. answer B. Finite-n caveat is the O(1) absolute loss E[ΔS]=θ∑ q^k/k = θ[-log(1-q)]>0 from the k=O(1) rare tail, which is o(a_n) relative to E[S]∼θ log n and vanishes relatively as n→∞.

Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7 argue the integrated infinite-sites view. Under infinite sites E[N_k]=θ/k, the expected absolute loss of segregating sites on V is θ[-log(1-q)]>0 independent of n. A singleton is lost with probability q, a doubleton with q², etc. The “no completely missing SNV’’ condition is a pre-filter property of V; after independent per-sample deletion a site can become monomorphic reference in the completed alignments when the few carriers in the panel are exactly the samples where the site is filtered. Because imputation is state-dependent – a derived allele can only be turned to reference – E[S_obs]=∑[1-q^{k_i}] < S_true in expectation, so E[θ̂_W,obs]=E[S_obs]/a_n < S_true/a_n on V. Hence both S-based θ_W and frequency-weighted π are systematically reduced, i.e. answer C.

Colleague 4 notes a strict set-theoretic nuance: fixed-derived sites f=1 are non-segregating in truth but can become artefactual segregating sites under deletion, Pr{segregating|f=1}→1 and E[π|f=1]=2r(1-r)>0, which would inflate S upward on a genome-wide per-base scale.

Unresolved is the intended reading of “the number of samples is arbitrarily large”. Under the fixed-p pointwise limit the textbook robust-to-missingness statement is B: π is systematically down-biased by reference imputation, θ̂_W is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained SNV set V. In the integrated spectrum/operational expectation sense both estimators are downward biased, C, with the relative bias of θ_W vanishing like O(1/log n) while the π bias persists. The problem phrasing and the no-completely-missing ascertainment point toward the n→∞ fixed-p idealisation, i.e. the B statement with the acknowledged finite-sample rare-allele loss as the practical caveat behind the C camp.

E[diff_obs|p]=2 r p[1−r p] < 2p(1−p)

site by site. Reference imputation turns every filtered derived copy into a reference match, so π_i^obs=2p_i^obs(1−p_i^obs)<2p_i(1−p_i).
